children: , the global payments network, introduced new tools to evaluate AI-driven purchases, with shares at $558.71, down approximately 0.86% at 11am ET on September 30. The services pull together identity, purchase intent, behavior and fraud signals. The central question is simple: does this shopping agent have permission to spend your money? As software takes over more of the checkout process, verifying that permission becomes a bigger part of payment security.

The first service tested in the U.S. estimates the likelihood that an AI agent initiated a transaction. Mastercard is also working with Cloudflare and Skyfire on agent verification as shared trust standards take shape. In its announcement, Mastercard projects that one in ten consumers could routinely use shopping agents by 2030. That could widen demand for verification services. But projected adoption is a starting point, not booked revenue.

The valuation picture puts shares 18.6% below the $686.34 GF Value estimatea potential discount that still needs a business case. These tools could help issuers separate authorized purchases from impersonation, but identifying an AI transaction does not automatically create another payment. The commercial test is tougher: consumers must adopt shopping agents, customers must pay for verification, and the tools must deliver measurable fraud reductions. Mastercard has a new service to sell. Adoption and revenue will determine its weight.

title: Mastercard Stocks Fall as AI Transactions Gain a Probability Score
